channel.title: Computer Chronicle
channel.description: A weekly early-1980s computer newspaper rebuilt from the historical record — games, software, hardware, prices, charts, and culture, one week at a time.

item.title: Week of October 28-November 3, 1985 — Hacker leaves players alone at the logon prompt
item.description: Activision turns a simulated computer connection into a mystery without a rule book. A computer connection appears to be going wrong. Activision president Jim Levy struggles to reach headquarters, then reveals that the apparent remote session is the game itself. October’s COMPUTE! recounts the demonstration in its fall-games survey: Hacker makes uncertainty its opening attraction, rather than a problem to be explained away in a manual. Also this week: Atari’s $799 desktop puts a mouse and 512K within reach · Amiga promises PC software without an 8088 board · 2400-bit modems become an affordable step up.

item.title: Week of October 21-27, 1985 — Winter Games brings snow and ice to the Commodore
item.description: Epyx turns the home computer into a seven-event winter arena, with October reviewers cheering from the sidelines. Epyx is taking its sporting competition into colder country. Winter Games, reviewed for the Commodore 64 in October’s Computer Entertainer, offers a winter counterpart to Summer Games and Summer Games II. The newsletter gives it four out of four for both graphics and play value. This is a game on the current month’s review desk, not a claim of a release on a particular day this week. Also this week: GEnie courts the home-computer caller · Atari puts a mouse-driven desktop below $1,000 · Nintendo keeps its New York experiment local.

item.title: Week of October 14-20, 1985 — Nintendo bets on New York with a new home-game system
item.description: A robot, a light gun and a cautious test market give the living-room console another chance. Nintendo is bringing its Entertainment System to the New York area in a mid-October test of American appetite for home video games. Computer Entertainer reports that the introduction is on schedule. Rather than promise an immediate national comeback for consoles, the company is starting with a single metropolitan market. Also this week: Intel introduces the 32-bit 80386 · Atari 520ST brings a mouse desktop under $800 · Fall games trade instructions for discovery and richer simulations.

item.title: Week of October 7-13, 1985 — No manual, no map: Hacker makes the software chart
item.description: Activision’s simulated mystery connection enters Billboard at No.7. An unexplained connection is finding an audience. Hacker enters the computer-software chart in Billboard dated October 12 at No.7, marked NEW and described as a Mystery Adventure Game. It is a sales-chart arrival, not a newly established release date, but it gives the season’s most unusual keyboard puzzle a place alongside familiar flight simulations. Also this week: Commodore 128 reaches British shops as Amiga courts developers · Apple–Digital Research dispute changes GEM’s screen furniture · Amstrad’s computer gamble drives record profits.

item.title: Week of September 30-October 6, 1985 — Hacker turns a mysterious computer connection into the game
item.description: Activision makes the unknown system itself the puzzle in October’s fall-game reports. The screen appears to have gone wrong. At a press demonstration described in October’s COMPUTE!, Activision president Jim Levy seems to struggle with a computer logon. Then comes the reveal: “That, ladies and gentlemen, is the game.” Hacker makes that uncertainty its opening invitation. Also this week: Winter Games takes the Epyx sports formula onto snow and ice · Atari’s 520ST puts a mouse-driven 512K system below $1,000 · Sinclair creditors back a Christmas survival campaign.

item.title: Week of September 23-29, 1985 — Apple takes Steve Jobs to court over his new computer venture
item.description: A $5-million suit turns the cofounder’s new venture into a legal battleground. Apple sued Steve Jobs on September 23, escalating the dispute surrounding its departed cofounder and his new computer venture. The Los Angeles Times reports the action in its September 24 edition under a headline describing a $5-million lawsuit. Also this week: Lucasfilm’s delayed games reach Atari owners through Epyx · Amiga review makes the case for a multimedia personal computer · Atari’s ST roadmap promises cheaper machines and compact-disc storage.

item.title: Week of September 16-22, 1985 — Jobs resigns from Apple
item.description: Cofounder leaves the chairmanship and turns toward a higher-education computer venture. Steve Jobs has resigned as chairman of Apple Computer. His September 17 letter to A. C. Markkula Jr., reproduced in the September 18 Mercury News, brings a formal break between the 30-year-old cofounder and the company he helped build. A proposed new venture aimed at higher education now occupies his attention. Also this week: Ultima IV makes virtue the object of the adventure · Amiga promises a multimedia desktop, but buyers must separate promise from delivery · A modem becomes a route to college credit · Britain gives computer programs explicit copyright protection.

item.title: Week of September 9-15, 1985 — Super Mario Bros. arrives on Japan’s Famicom
item.description: Nintendo sends Mario across a scrolling Mushroom Kingdom on September 13. Japan’s Famicom has a new adventure this Friday, September 13: Nintendo’s Super Mario Bros. The cartridge puts running and jumping at the center of a journey through the Mushroom Kingdom, giving Mario a landscape of obstacles rather than a single fixed screen. This is the Japanese release; it is not a simultaneous worldwide launch. Also this week: Jobs tells Apple board he intends to start another computer company · COMPUTE! puts the Amiga under the microscope · Atari ST expansion promises fill the autumn calendar.

item.title: Week of September 2-8, 1985 — Amiga opens a new frontier in color and sound
item.description: Commodore’s 68000 machine brings multitasking and custom graphics into the home-computer debate. A personal computer that can keep several jobs moving while drawing colorful scenes and playing stereo sound is a different proposition from the familiar single-program machine. Tom R. Halfhill’s September COMPUTE! examination of the already unveiled Amiga describes Commodore’s bid to make that proposition practical. It is a report from prerelease sessions, not a new unveiling this week. Also this week: Lucasfilm games escape limbo through Epyx · SIG wars ask who owns an online community · Powerhouse promises home control without leaving the computer on.

item.title: Week of August 26-September 1, 1985 — Archon II: Adept makes every spell count
item.description: Free Fall’s fantasy contest trades familiar territory for an elemental struggle over energy. Archon II: Adept brings the meeting of strategy and arcade combat back to the home computer, but not as a simple second helping of the original board. Arthur Leyenberger’s review in the August COMPUTE! describes a contest built around magical energy and the four elements. Electronic Arts publishes the Free Fall Associates game. Also this week: Atari puts an encyclopedia on an optical disc · WordPerfect makes a blank screen its selling point · Behind the SIG, an online business.

item.title: Week of August 19-25, 1985 — Amiga and Atari ST bring color and a new price war to the showroom
item.description: Two mouse-driven 68000 machines promise more picture for the money, but stock and software demand a close look. The new color-computer contest is moving from announcements to dealer showrooms. In his August 19 Los Angeles Times column, Richard O’Reilly compares the Atari 520ST and Commodore Amiga as bargains worth hunting down. That last qualification matters: shoppers may still have trouble finding a machine to examine. This is a market comparison, not a fresh launch announcement. Also this week: Lucasfilm puts sport and mountain rescue on the Atari · ST software makers race to fill the new machine’s shelves · Adventure Master turns players into authors.

item.title: Week of August 12-18, 1985 — Lucasfilm brings the movie studio’s flair to Atari game screens
item.description: Ballblazer and Rescue on Fractalus bring split-screen sport and mountain rescue to the Atari disk drive. Lucasfilm’s long-awaited Atari games receive an enthusiastic examination in the August Antic. Michael Ciraolo reviews Ballblazer and Rescue on Fractalus, distributed by Epyx, at $40 apiece for 48K Atari disk systems. These are this month’s review-room attractions, not newly dated launches for the week. Also this week: Atari puts an encyclopedia on an optical disc · The ST’s next test is software, not specifications · A construction set for the neighborhood bulletin board.

item.title: Week of August 5-11, 1985 — Archon II: Adept brings a new war of magic to home computers
item.description: Electronic Arts’ strategy-and-action sequel earns an enthusiastic August review. The battlefield is magical, but the accounting is exacting. Archon II: Adept, developed by Free Fall Associates and published by Electronic Arts, earns an enthusiastic review from Arthur Leyenberger in August’s COMPUTE! The sequel keeps the mixture of strategic planning and real-time fighting while changing the armies and the decisions that sustain them. Also this week: Epyx lines up winter sports, Lucasfilm adventures and a dungeon trilogy · Atari demonstrates an encyclopedia on one optical disc · Commodore fills out the 128’s peripheral shelf.

item.title: Week of July 29-August 4, 1985 — Acorn saved again as Olivetti raises its stake to 78.9%
item.description: BBC Micro maker avoids liquidation in its second rescue package of the year. Acorn has been saved from liquidation by a complex financial restructuring, according to the August 1 issue of Popular Computing Weekly. The magazine describes the arrangement as the BBC Micro maker’s second rescue package of the year, with Olivetti increasing its stake to 78.9 percent. Also this week: The Way of the Exploding Fist earns its five stars · HomePak brings three jobs to one disk · WordStar heads for the Amstrad CPC.

item.title: Week of July 22-28, 1985 — Amiga takes the stage: Commodore bets on color and creativity
item.description: A $1,295 computer makes its New York debut, with September shipments promised. Commodore unveiled its Amiga on July 23 at the Vivian Beaumont Theater in New York’s Lincoln Center. The Motorola 68000-based computer arrives with a striking brief: make color graphics, sound and creative work central to the personal-computer experience. The announced computer price is $1,295; that figure should not be confused with a monitor-inclusive package. Also this week: Kennedy Approach puts talking aircraft on the home-computer radar · Atari 130XE keeps 8-bit compatibility while doubling memory · One disk, three jobs: HomePak courts the home office.

item.title: Week of July 15-21, 1985 — British Telecom prepares MUD 2: shared adventures by telephone
item.description: A commercial multiplayer adventure is planned for September, with forty lines to start. British Telecom is preparing to turn the shared computer adventure into a commercial telephone service. Popular Computing Weekly reports on July 18 that MUD 2 is being developed for a planned unveiling at September’s Personal Computer World Show. This is a service in preparation, not a July opening. Also this week: Sinclair puts its name on a floppy drive for the QL · Credit-card software takes aim at tapes and piracy · Amstrad 6128 may reach Britain this autumn.

item.title: Week of July 8-14, 1985 — Atari 520ST reaches buyers as the 16-bit contest intensifies
item.description: July shipping news brings a powerful new desktop into the summer contest, with Commodore’s unveiling still ahead. The Atari 520ST is moving from demonstration promise to the buyer’s desk. The New York Times carries a July 10 shipping report, while the machine’s widening July availability marks a new stage in the contest for the personal-computer household. This is not the original unveiling: limited releases have preceded the broader summer arrival. Also this week: Activision puts the Tour de France on home micros · Compact discs promise encyclopedia-sized storage for home micros · Dixons cuts MSX prices to £99 and £149.99 · Acorn’s financial strain stalls new projects.

item.title: Week of July 1-7, 1985 — SSI ventures into arcade adventure with Gemstone Warrior
item.description: A war-game specialist sends Apple and Commodore players underground. Strategic Simulations Inc., best known for detailed war games, is trying a different sort of battle. James V. Trunzo’s July COMPUTE! review finds Gemstone Warrior an arcade-oriented adventure in which fast decisions and quick reflexes matter more than the patient calculations of a historical simulation. This is a current review, not a claim that the game first appeared this week. Also this week: Atari prepares the ST for summer buyers · HomePak bundles writing, filing and telecommunications for $49.95 · The online information boom comes with a running meter.

item.title: Week of June 24-30, 1985 — Apple cuts one-fifth of workforce as first quarterly loss looms
item.description: Three plants face closure as the personal-computer maker lowers its break-even point. Apple Computer is cutting 1,200 jobs and closing three of its six production plants, according to the June 24 Computerworld. The recently announced restructuring removes roughly one-fifth of the workforce as the company prepares for what it expects will be its first quarterly loss in eight years. Also this week: Electronic novels recruit poets as well as science-fiction stars · Commodore 128 promises three computing worlds in one box · Commodore LCD portable slips beyond September.

item.title: Week of June 17-23, 1985 — Elite brings its trading galaxy to the Commodore 64
item.description: Firebird’s space-trading adventure gains colour on another home micro, with a few changes at the docking bay. The Commodore 64 has a new galaxy to explore. Martin Croft’s review in the June 20–26 Popular Computing Weekly finds Elite available from Firebird, carrying across the space-trading and combat formula that made it a major BBC and Electron success in 1984. The review establishes its arrival by this week’s issue, rather than a precise launch day. Also this week: Sinclair faces a Maxwell rescue and a smaller role for Sir Clive · Atari courts more than 100 British software houses for the ST · Dixons keeps the Plus/4 below £100 despite Commodore’s bundling push.
